 Media deal money is chasing assets that gather fans
 BRIEF Sports teams, venues, franchise IP and fan data command a premium in U.S. media deals, as investors back assets that draw fans and monetize them through tickets, rights and ads. As Korea adds venues and bids for rights, the question is who keeps the fan relationship.
 Jung Han 
 November 17, 2026 
 11 min read분 읽기 
 Fandom is the thread running through the Lakers, Cosm and LiveRamp deals… for Korea, the question is how to earn money after securing venues and media rights
 BRIEF  Sports teams, venues, franchise IP and fan data command a premium in U.S. media deals, as investors back assets that draw fans and monetize them through tickets, rights and ads. As Korea adds venues and bids for rights, the question is who keeps the fan relationship. U.S. media companies and investors are pouring money into businesses that meet fans directly. They are buying sports teams, investing in venues and immersive theaters, and acquiring data companies that link audiences' tastes and purchase histories. The targets differ, but the math is similar: secure a reason for fans to come, then harvest ticket, media-rights and advertising revenue from that relationship for years.
 The clearest example came in August, when venture investor Josh Kushner and former Disney CEO Bob Iger agreed to buy the NBA's Los Angeles Lakers at a $12.5 billion valuation. That was 25% above the $10 billion valuation at which Mark Walter took control in October 2025, just 10 months earlier.
 Axios reported on Nov. 14 , citing investment bankers, that media M&A demand is converging on sports, live events, franchise intellectual property and consumer data. A popular team's game or a particular artist's concert can't be supplied elsewhere at the same time. If the owner can also sell tickets directly to fans and learn their tastes and purchase histories, a one-off hit can turn into the next sale.
 Buyers are also looking beyond venues to ticketing, production technology and event hospitality and travel services. Alex Michael, global head of sports and entertainment at media investment bank LionTree, told Axios he believes in investing in offline experiences — the so-called "analog trade." Companies are widening their reach to the places where content is consumed and the customers who show up there.
 Paramount Skydance completed its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery on Oct. 6. French ad group Publicis Groupe bought data-connectivity platform LiveRamp for about $2.2 billion on Nov. 2. Sony Pictures Entertainment invested in Cosm, which runs immersive screening venues. Studio IP, the places audiences gather and the data that measures advertising results each sat at the center of a deal.
 The Lakers deal is agreed; Letterboxd is in exclusive talks. On Location reflects TKO's 2025 $3.25 billion package deal. Sources: Axios, company announcements, press reports The live market grows, but valuations diverge
 Revenue across cinema, live music, out-of-home advertising and trade shows reached about $149 billion in 2025, nearly double 2021, according to consultancy PwC, which projects about $174 billion by 2030. PwC partner Bart Spiegel says attending concerts and games has become "social currency" that younger consumers use to present themselves on Instagram and TikTok. Shared on social media, the experience brings in the next audience.
 Selling in-person experiences doesn't guarantee a rich valuation, though. In an Axios comparison of stock performance from August 2021 to August 2026, the S&P 500 rose in the 70% range, Sphere about 350% and IMAX more than 200%. AMC Entertainment and ticket reseller Vivid Seats lost most of their value, and companies with theme park businesses, including Disney, Comcast and Six Flags, lagged. Six Flags saw attendance and earnings fall after raising prices, and one operator of the much-copied "Immersive Van Gogh" exhibitions went bankrupt in 2023. What separated winners from losers was whether the experience was distinctive enough for audiences to pay extra.
 Monthly closing prices, Aug. 2021–Aug. 2026. Values are approximations read from Axios charts. Source: Financial Modeling Prep via Axios The price of fandom on teams and new leagues
 The Lakers deal still needs NBA owner approval. Walter, the seller, joined Clear Channel Outdoor's $6.2 billion take-private in October as a co-investor. The Cadillac F1 team in which he holds a majority stake is also selling equity. Fenway Sports Group is among the suitors, The Wall Street Journal reported , and Walter's side values the team at more than $3 billion.
 The money has spread to women's sports and new leagues. NWSL club Gotham FC raised $100 million at a $350 million valuation, 84% above Forbes' April estimate. New women's basketball league Unrivaled launched with a TNT Sports deal and more than 20 brand partners. The International Dance League (IDL) signed its first media-rights deal with ESPN and aired its Aug. 27 Seoul event on ESPN2 — an attempt to turn the profile of dancers who have worked with artists such as BTS into teams, seasons and regular competitions.
 Why content companies are investing in screens and venues
 Sony Pictures made a $100 million strategic investment in Cosm on June 24. Having bought theater chain Alamo Drafthouse in 2024, it now has both conventional cinemas and immersive domes in its business base. Maryland's Prince George's County gave final approval on Oct. 27 to a 6,000-seat Sphere at National Harbor outside Washington, a $1.4 billion project backed by $215 million in county bonds. Premium screens are proving profitable too: IMAX's average U.S. adult ticket costs $20.57, more than 60% above a standard ticket's $12.75, yet Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" earned more than $400 million in IMAX alone.
 A rendering of the planned Sphere at National Harbor, Maryland, slated to open in early 2030. Image: Prince George's County Roofs on football stadiums reflect the same business logic. Nine NFL teams are spending about $20 billion to build or renovate stadiums, and at least six of the nine projects include a dome or large canopy. The Tennessee Titans plan to open a $2.2 billion fixed-roof stadium in early 2027, and the Cleveland Browns are pursuing a $2.6 billion, 67,500-seat dome. Super Bowl sites set through 2030 — Inglewood, Atlanta, Las Vegas and Nashville — all have roofs. Taking weather out of the equation lets a stadium host concerts and events such as college basketball's Final Four beyond football. To recoup the investment, the building has to be full on non-game days too.
 The race for IP brings heavier acquisition debt
 In studio deals, the financial burden after closing has grown along with the value of the IP acquired. The combined Skydance now owns the Paramount, Warner Bros. and Skydance film studios, Paramount+ and HBO Max, and CNN and CBS. Paramount raised $52 billion in new debt for the deal, some of it yielding nearly 9%. Yahoo also sold bonds yielding 11% to repay debt from Apollo's buyout. If more assets don't bring in matching cash, interest costs can squeeze room to run the business.
 Companies are taking on that burden to secure rights that generate revenue for years. Legendary Entertainment made an offer in October for Lionsgate , owner of "The Hunger Games" and "John Wick," whose library brings in about $1 billion a year. BMG combined with Concord in September, securing a catalog of more than 4 million works. Comcast said in June it will separate NBCUniversal and Sky into a standalone public company, and an investor has proposed taking Roblox, worth about $35 billion, private . Strategies to gather rights through acquisitions are running alongside moves to restructure companies so their assets are revalued.
 Data deals that connect fans' tastes and purchases
 Data that shows what fans watch and what they spend money on is also a prime target. LiveRamp is a data collaboration platform linking more than 25,000 publisher domains across 14 markets. Rival ad agencies raised concerns about shared infrastructure passing into Publicis' hands, and the FTC required LiveRamp to remain neutral for five years . Ad tech company Infillion bought location-data firm Foursquare in September; linking ad exposure with store-visit and purchase data makes it easier to show advertisers what their spending achieved.
 The New York Times Company is in exclusive talks to buy film fan community Letterboxd for about $330 million — more than 20 times this year's projected EBITDA. Users have grown from 1.8 million in 2020 to about 30 million . Their reviews and ratings are content that draws in other fans and, at the same time, data on film tastes. Sony and A24 also showed interest . Staying in touch with moviegoers without buying the rights to films is a different approach from buying a studio.
 In Korea, what comes after building venues now matters
 U.S. deal assets and Korean counterparts 
 Asset type Key U.S. deals Korean counterpart 
 Sports teams and rights Lakers at $12.5B (agreed); Gotham FC valued at $350M CJ ENM exclusive KBO streaming rights (2027–2031) 
 Venues and immersive spaces Sony Pictures' $100M Cosm investment; Clear Channel Outdoor $6.2B take-private Seoul Arena opening 2027; national flagship concert hall site selection 
 Franchise IP Paramount–Warner $111B merger; Legendary's offer for Lionsgate Kakao Entertainment and SM Entertainment merge North American units 
 First-party data Publicis–LiveRamp $2.2B; NYT–Letterboxd $330M talks TVING's KBO viewing and subscription data (paid subscribers up 24.7%) 
 Sources: Axios, company announcements, press reports Korea's large-scale concerts and new facilities are growing together. Performance ticket sales tallied by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Arts Management Service through KOPIS rose 18.8% in 2025 to 1.7326 trillion won ($1.3 billion). Popular music grew 29% to 981.7 billion won ($736 million), the largest genre, led by shows of 10,000 seats or more. The average ticket price rose about 5,000 won in a year to roughly 70,000 won, and first-half 2026 pop-music ticket sales reached 452.7 billion won.
 2024 popular-music figure is an approximation back-calculated from 2025 sales and 29% growth. Source: Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and Korea Arts Management Service (KOPIS) Facilities have also shifted where audiences travel. Seoul's share of national ticket sales fell from 65.1% in 2024 to 60.6% in 2025, while Gyeonggi rose from 8.7% to 14.5% and Incheon from 5.2% to 7.6%. The KOPIS report pointed to more venues and more large shows in Gyeonggi and Incheon. Big K-pop concerts have mostly been held in rented stadiums and arenas — Seoul Olympic Stadium, Seoul World Cup Stadium, Gocheok Sky Dome and the KSPO Dome. With few dedicated concert halls, available dates have been a constraint agencies must plan tours around from the start.
 Large K-pop concerts in Korea have relied on renting outdoor stadiums and indoor domes and arenas. Source: Segye Ilbo (July 30, 2026) Seoul Arena, a dedicated pop-music venue under construction in Changdong, Seoul, is scheduled to open in 2027 . Right after opening, in December, it will serve as the main stage for "Fanomenon," the K-culture festival of the presidential Popular Culture Exchange Committee. The city has proposed hosting more than 100 concerts a year , and the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism is moving to choose a site for a national flagship concert hall. Since CJ Live City's arena project in Goyang collapsed , attention has turned to alternatives that ease the venue shortage.
 The Jamsil sports and MICE complex faces the same test. Jamsil Baseball Stadium, opened in 1982, closed after the LG Twins–KIA Tigers semi-playoff Game 3 on Oct. 20. Seoul plans a 30,000-seat domed ballpark and a convention center 2.5 times the size of COEX. The project cleared private-investment review in July , with construction slated for the second half and completion targeted for 2032, at a cost of 3.3 trillion won . Just as Gocheok Sky Dome hosts K-pop concerts and award shows in the off-season, how many non-baseball events the new Jamsil dome can book will determine its profitability. As with NFL stadiums, the year-round operating plan matters as much as the build.
 In sports rights, repeat viewing turns into subscription revenue. CJ ENM secured exclusive KBO League streaming rights for 2027–2031. The previous 2024–2026 deal was 135 billion won over three years , or 45 billion won a year — more than double the 22 billion won a year paid by the earlier telecom-portal consortium. The new deal's value was not disclosed. In 2026 the KBO League passed 10 million fans in a record-fast 565 games , and TVING's paid subscribers rose 24.7% from a year earlier. The business value of rights depends on how much sign-up and return visits they drive, not just viewing.
 2024–2026 shows the annual average of the three-year 135 billion won deal; the 2027–2031 value is undisclosed. Source: CJ ENM, industry estimates In music, Kakao Entertainment and SM Entertainment agreed to merge their North American units , putting the planning, production and distribution of artist IP under one organization — a move to build a structure that can keep commercializing their IP in the local market.
 The same approach could apply to dance. Mnet's "Street Woman Fighter" built dance crews' profiles and fandoms; IDL runs a regular league that bundles teams, seasons, media rights and brand partners. Korean agencies and broadcasters could design businesses so that a crew's popularity carries on into concerts and competitions after a show ends, with league stakes or co-hosted events as possible routes.
 Broadcasters must design their live assets beyond the broadcast
 In the AI era, what matters for broadcasters is not only where they show live content but what relationship they keep with fans afterward. KBO games still air on terrestrial and sports channels, but online live streaming has centered on TVING since 2024. Game-by-game viewing histories and sign-up and churn data accumulate with whoever runs the online service. Delivering the same game, the two sides end up with very different ability to know customers and offer them the next product.
 Music-show tapings, year-end award shows and big concert broadcasts are also broadcaster assets where fans gather at a set time. To carry them beyond a single airing into ticket sales, fan participation and follow-up shows, broadcasters need to settle rights and data-use terms with venues and platforms from the planning stage. Sony's Cosm investment shows a content company taking a stake in the place where it meets its audience. When co-producing with new venues and events, Korean broadcasters should negotiate not only production fees and rights fees but also ticket revenue shares, rights to follow-on businesses and the scope for using consented customer data.
 Success in the next deals will be decided after closing
 Major deals under negotiation or review 
 Asset Potential buyer Reported value Status 
 Letterboxd The New York Times Company ~$330M Exclusive talks (reported Nov. 5) 
 LA Sparks and training facility TBD $700M+ (asking) Sale process (reported Oct. 23) 
 Cadillac F1 team stake Fenway Sports Group, others Team valued at ~$3B Majority-stake talks (reported Nov. 4) 
 Lionsgate Legendary Entertainment Undisclosed Offer submitted (reported Oct. 20) 
 IMAX TBD Undisclosed Sale review (reported May)

 SeatGeek IPO Undisclosed Confidential IPO filing (reported Aug.) 
 Sources: The New York Times, Bloomberg, The Boston Globe, The Wall Street Journal The Letterboxd talks, the LA Sparks sale, the Cadillac F1 stake talks and Legendary's offer for Lionsgate are still unresolved. IMAX's sale review and the change in Liberty Media's voting structure are also variables for the deal market. Whether negotiated prices hold through to final deals, and what operating strategies new owners bring, remain to be seen.
 These deals also leave Korea's industry with work to do. Even after Seoul Arena opens and the new KBO rights deal begins, securing facilities and rights alone won't guarantee revenue. Venues need the programming capacity to fill empty dates; rights holders need services that keep fans around all season. Content producers and broadcasters must also choose between simply taking production fees and sharing in ticket and follow-on revenue. Korean content has the power to draw fans; it is time to design contracts and business structures so that it also earns from its relationship with them.
